query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance and microscopic deformation of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate during sliding in the high-temperature operating regime are governed by the activation of different slip systems and the formation of nanotwins, which are influenced by the alloy's composition, processing, and deformation history.

generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between alloy composition, processing, and deformation history and the resulting wear resistance and microscopic deformation is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear resistance and microscopic deformation do not correlate with the predicted outcomes based on the activation of different slip systems and the formation of nanotwins, the hypothesis is falsified

We unveil the underlying deformation mechanism and mechanistic origins of the ultrahigh uniform tensile ductility through in situ TEM, scanning TEM (STEM) atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging, and large-scale atomistic simulations. cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.
